'''Wilfried Schmid''' (born May 28, 1943) is a German-born American mathematician who works in [[Hodge theory]], [[representation theory]], and [[automorphic form]]s.

Schmid was raised in [[Bonn]] where his father {{ill|Wolfgang Schmid (classicist)|lt=Wolfgang Schmid|de|Wolfgang Schmid (Philologe)}} (1913–1980) served as a professor of [[classics]].  In 1960, Schmid followed his father to [[Princeton, New Jersey|Princeton]] when the latter was a fellow at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]]. After graduating as valedictorian<ref>{{Cite web |title=Princeton Names Speakers |url=https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1964/04/14/106958704.html?pageNumber=22 |access-date=2022-08-12 |website=timesmachine.nytimes.com |language=en}}</ref> of [[Princeton University]]'s class of 1964, Schmid earned his [[Ph.D.]] at [[University of California, Berkeley]] in 1967 under the direction of [[Phillip Griffiths]], and then taught at Berkeley and [[Columbia University]], becoming a full professor at Columbia at age 27.  In 1978, he moved to [[Harvard University]], where he served as the Dwight Parker Robinson Professor of Mathematics until his retirement in 2019.<ref name=bio> [https://web.archive.org/web/20120523184152/http://www2.ed.gov/about/bdscomm/list/mathpanel/bios/schmid.html Biography of Dr. Wilfried Schmid], U.S. Department of Education via [[Wayback Machine]].</ref>

Schmid's early work concerns the construction of [[discrete series representation]]s of semi-simple [[Lie group]]s.  Notable accomplishments here include a proof of the [[Langlands conjecture]] on the [[discrete series]], along with a later proof (joint with [[Michael Atiyah]]) constructing all such discrete series representations on spaces of harmonic spinors.  Schmid, along with his student Henryk Hecht, proved [[Blattner's conjecture]] in 1975.  In the 1970s, he described the singularities of the Griffith's period map by applying [[Lie theory|Lie-theoretic method]]s to problems in [[algebraic geometry]].<ref name=nas>[https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/wilfried-schmid-tiy11j/ “Wilfried Schmid, Harvard University, Biosketch], National Academy of Sciences, retrieved 2022-05-22.</ref>

Schmid has been very involved in K–12 mathematics education in his home state, and both nationally and internationally.  His interest arose in 1999 after being disturbed by the experiences of his 2nd-grade daughter, Sabina, in her mathematics class.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Hartocollis |first=Anemona |date=2000-04-27 |title=The New, Flexible Math Meets Parental Rebellion |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2000/04/27/nyregion/the-new-flexible-math-meets-parental-rebellion.html |access-date=2022-08-12 |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>  He was heavily involved in the drafting of the Massachusetts Mathematics Curriculum Framework in 2000.  Later, he served on the National Mathematics Advisory Panel of the [[United States Department of Education|U.S. Department of Education]].<ref name=bio /> He has opposed new ways of teaching children that would neglect basic math skills.<ref>Schmid, Wilfried.  “[https://www.thecrimson.com/article/2000/5/4/new-battles-in-the-math-wars/ New Battles in the Math Wars]”, ''[[The Harvard Crimson]]'' (May 4, 2000).</ref>

In 2012, he became a fellow of the [[American Mathematical Society]]<ref>[http://www.ams.org/profession/fellows-list List of Fellows of the American Mathematical Society] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180825194636/http://www.ams.org/profession/fellows-list |date=2018-08-25 }}, retrieved 2013-07-14.</ref> and in 2020 he was elected as a member of the U.S. [[National Academy of Sciences]].<ref name=nas />
